---
title: Munich Solar & Battery Storage Economics
---

Since 2025, German electricity suppliers must offer *dynamic* tariffs indexed
to the [SMARD](https://www.smard.de) day-ahead spot price (§41a EnWG). This
demo asks: for a Munich household with rooftop solar on such a tariff, how
much does adding a **home battery** save — by storing surplus solar instead of
exporting it at the low, fixed feed-in tariff, and by covering evening demand
instead of buying at whatever the spot price happens to be that hour?

PV generation is modeled from real hourly irradiance at
[Weihenstephan-Dürnast](https://www.dwd.de) (DWD station 05404, ~30 km north
of Munich near Freising — the closest DWD radiation-measuring station, since
none exists inside the city itself). Grid cost is modeled from the real SMARD
DE-LU day-ahead price. Both are ingested by
[`munich_solar.py`](../reference/incremental.incremental.qmd) using
[`@incremental`](../reference/incremental.incremental.qmd) and
[`@schema`](../reference/schema.schema.qmd).

**Data sources:** SMARD / Bundesnetzagentur · DWD Climate Data Center ·
License: [Datenlizenz Deutschland – Namensnennung 2.0](https://www.govdata.de/dl-de/by-2-0)

```{python}
#| echo: false
import os

import altair as alt
import polars as pl

BUCKET = os.environ.get("MUNICH_CYCLING_BUCKET", "data-warehousing-with-polars")
```

## Loading and joining the raw data

```{python}
#| echo: false
price = pl.scan_delta(f"s3://{BUCKET}/delta/munich_solar_spot_price").select(
    "timestamp", "price_eur_mwh"
)
irradiance = pl.scan_delta(f"s3://{BUCKET}/delta/munich_solar_irradiance").select(
    "datetime_utc", "ghi_kwh_per_m2"
)

hourly = (
    price.with_columns(
        pl.col("timestamp").dt.replace_time_zone(None).cast(pl.Datetime("us")).alias("hour")
    )
    .join(irradiance, left_on="hour", right_on="datetime_utc", how="inner")
    .sort("hour")
    .collect()
)
hourly.drop_nulls().tail(5)
```

## Modeling PV generation and household load

Generation is estimated for a fixed, typical German residential system —
**8 kWp**, 85% performance ratio — as `irradiance × capacity × performance
ratio`. This ignores panel tilt, orientation, and temperature derating, which
a real yield estimate would include.

Household consumption uses a synthetic diurnal profile (morning and evening
peaks, a midday and overnight trough) applied identically every day and
scaled to **4,000 kWh/year**, typical for a 2–3 person household. This is a
simplification too: it ignores weekday/weekend and seasonal shape that a real
smart-meter profile would show.

```{python}
#| echo: false
CAPACITY_KWP = 8.0
PERFORMANCE_RATIO = 0.85
ANNUAL_LOAD_KWH = 4000.0

# Synthetic hourly load-shape weights (00:00 .. 23:00) — morning + evening peaks.
_LOAD_WEIGHTS = [
    0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.25, 0.40, 0.70, 1.00,
    0.80, 0.60, 0.50, 0.50, 0.55, 0.50, 0.50, 0.60,
    0.80, 1.20, 1.60, 1.80, 1.50, 1.10, 0.70, 0.45,
]
_weight_sum = sum(_LOAD_WEIGHTS)
load_shape = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "hour_of_day": list(range(24)),
        "load_kwh": [w / _weight_sum * ANNUAL_LOAD_KWH / 365.0 for w in _LOAD_WEIGHTS],
    }
)

sim = (
    hourly.with_columns(pl.col("hour").dt.hour().alias("hour_of_day"))
    .join(load_shape, on="hour_of_day", how="left")
    .with_columns(
        (pl.col("ghi_kwh_per_m2") * CAPACITY_KWP * PERFORMANCE_RATIO).alias("generation_kwh")
    )
    .with_columns((pl.col("generation_kwh") - pl.col("load_kwh")).alias("net_kwh"))
    .drop_nulls(["net_kwh", "price_eur_mwh"])
    .sort("hour")
)

correlation = sim.select(pl.corr("generation_kwh", "price_eur_mwh")).item()
print(f"Annual generation: {sim['generation_kwh'].sum():,.0f} kWh")
print(f"Annual load:       {sim['load_kwh'].sum():,.0f} kWh")
print(f"Corr(generation, spot price): {correlation:.2f}")
```

This is the mismatch a battery gets paid to fix: PV output peaks around
midday, while the assumed household load profile peaks in the morning and,
more sharply, in the evening. Without storage, most solar generation happens
when nobody's home to use it.

```{python}
#| echo: false
avg_generation_by_hour = (
    sim.group_by("hour_of_day")
    .agg(pl.col("generation_kwh").mean().alias("Average PV generation"))
    .sort("hour_of_day")
)
profile = load_shape.rename({"load_kwh": "Household load (assumed)"}).join(
    avg_generation_by_hour, on="hour_of_day"
)
profile_long = profile.unpivot(
    index="hour_of_day",
    on=["Household load (assumed)", "Average PV generation"],
    variable_name="series",
    value_name="kwh",
)

alt.Chart(profile_long).mark_line(point=True).encode(
    x=alt.X("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour of day"),
    y=alt.Y("kwh:Q", title="kWh"),
    color=alt.Color(
        "series:N",
        title=None,
        scale=alt.Scale(
            domain=["Household load (assumed)", "Average PV generation"],
            range=["#4C78A8", "#F2A83A"],
        ),
    ),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour"),
        alt.Tooltip("series:N", title="Series"),
        alt.Tooltip("kwh:Q", title="kWh", format=".2f"),
    ],
).properties(width="container", height=240).configure_view(strokeWidth=0)
```

## Simulating battery sizes

State of charge is path-dependent, so this walks the hourly `generation −
load` series **sequentially in Python** for each candidate battery size
(0–15 kWh) — surplus charges the battery up to its capacity and any
remainder is exported; a deficit discharges the battery and any remainder is
bought from the grid at that hour's spot price. Each battery size reduces to
three totals: grid purchase volume, its spot-market cost, and un-stored
export volume.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def simulate_battery(battery_kwh: float, nets: list[float], prices_mwh: list[float]):
    soc = 0.0
    deficit_kwh = 0.0
    spot_cost_eur = 0.0
    export_kwh = 0.0
    for net, price_mwh in zip(nets, prices_mwh):
        if net >= 0:
            charge = min(net, battery_kwh - soc)
            soc += charge
            export_kwh += net - charge
        else:
            need = -net
            discharge = min(need, soc)
            soc -= discharge
            remaining = need - discharge
            deficit_kwh += remaining
            spot_cost_eur += remaining * price_mwh / 1000.0
    return deficit_kwh, spot_cost_eur, export_kwh


_nets = sim["net_kwh"].to_list()
_prices = sim["price_eur_mwh"].to_list()

battery_scenarios = pl.DataFrame(
    [
        dict(
            zip(
                ("battery_kwh", "deficit_kwh", "spot_cost_eur", "export_kwh"),
                (b, *simulate_battery(float(b), _nets, _prices)),
            )
        )
        for b in range(16)
    ]
)

# Carry the no-battery baseline onto every row so the interactive chart can
# recompute "savings vs. no battery" for any slider values without re-running
# the simulation in the browser.
_baseline = battery_scenarios.filter(pl.col("battery_kwh") == 0).row(0, named=True)
battery_scenarios = battery_scenarios.with_columns(
    pl.lit(_baseline["deficit_kwh"]).alias("deficit_kwh_0"),
    pl.lit(_baseline["spot_cost_eur"]).alias("spot_cost_eur_0"),
    pl.lit(_baseline["export_kwh"]).alias("export_kwh_0"),
)
battery_scenarios.head(5)
```

## Battery economics — drag the sliders

Grid markup (taxes, grid fees, supplier margin on top of the spot price),
the statutory feed-in tariff for un-stored export, and battery installation
cost are all linear in the totals computed above, so the sliders below
recompute savings and payback live in the browser — no server, no
re-simulation.

```{python}
#| echo: false
markup_param = alt.param(
    name="markup_ct_per_kwh",
    value=20,
    bind=alt.binding_range(min=10, max=30, step=1, name="Grid markup (ct/kWh): "),
)
fit_param = alt.param(
    name="fit_ct_per_kwh",
    value=8,
    bind=alt.binding_range(min=0, max=15, step=0.5, name="Feed-in tariff (ct/kWh): "),
)
capex_param = alt.param(
    name="capex_eur_per_kwh",
    value=700,
    bind=alt.binding_range(min=400, max=1200, step=25, name="Battery cost (€/kWh): "),
)

base = (
    alt.Chart(battery_scenarios)
    .transform_calculate(
        total_cost=(
            "datum.spot_cost_eur + datum.deficit_kwh * markup_ct_per_kwh / 100"
            " - datum.export_kwh * fit_ct_per_kwh / 100"
        ),
        base_cost=(
            "datum.spot_cost_eur_0 + datum.deficit_kwh_0 * markup_ct_per_kwh / 100"
            " - datum.export_kwh_0 * fit_ct_per_kwh / 100"
        ),
    )
    .transform_calculate(savings_eur="datum.base_cost - datum.total_cost")
    .transform_calculate(
        payback_years=(
            "datum.battery_kwh == 0 ? null"
            " : (datum.battery_kwh * capex_eur_per_kwh) / datum.savings_eur"
        )
    )
)

savings_chart = base.mark_line(point=True, color="#4C78A8").encode(
    x=alt.X("battery_kwh:Q", title="Battery size (kWh)"),
    y=alt.Y("savings_eur:Q", title="Annual savings vs. no battery (€/yr)"),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("battery_kwh:Q", title="Battery (kWh)"),
        alt.Tooltip("savings_eur:Q", title="Savings (€/yr)", format=",.0f"),
    ],
).properties(width="container", height=200)

payback_chart = base.mark_line(point=True, color="#E45756").encode(
    x=alt.X("battery_kwh:Q", title="Battery size (kWh)"),
    y=alt.Y("payback_years:Q", title="Payback period (years)"),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("battery_kwh:Q", title="Battery (kWh)"),
        alt.Tooltip("payback_years:Q", title="Payback (years)", format=".1f"),
    ],
).properties(width="container", height=200)

(savings_chart | payback_chart).add_params(markup_param, fit_param, capex_param)
```

With the defaults above (a system oversized relative to this household's
demand, which is common when sized for future EV/heat-pump load), most of the
reachable savings show up in the first few kWh of storage — beyond that,
summer surplus already has nowhere to go, so extra capacity mostly sits idle
and payback gets worse, not better. Raising the feed-in tariff slider flattens
that curve, since idle capacity matters less when export pays more; raising
the markup slider steepens it, since covering evening demand from the battery
becomes more valuable relative to buying at spot.

## A day with the battery

The aggregate savings/payback curves above hide what actually happens hour by
hour. Pick a **day** and a **battery size** below to walk through it: how full
the battery gets, and whether that hour's demand was met directly from the
panels, from the battery, or bought from the grid.

```{python}
#| echo: false
def simulate_battery_trace(
    battery_kwh: float, gens: list[float], loads: list[float]
):
    soc = 0.0
    socs, self_consumption, charge, discharge, grid, export = [], [], [], [], [], []
    for gen, load in zip(gens, loads):
        net = gen - load
        direct = min(gen, load)
        if net >= 0:
            c = min(net, battery_kwh - soc)
            soc += c
            self_consumption.append(direct)
            charge.append(c)
            discharge.append(0.0)
            grid.append(0.0)
            export.append(net - c)
        else:
            need = -net
            d = min(need, soc)
            soc -= d
            self_consumption.append(direct)
            charge.append(0.0)
            discharge.append(d)
            grid.append(need - d)
            export.append(0.0)
        socs.append(soc)
    return socs, self_consumption, charge, discharge, grid, export


BATTERY_SIZES_KWH = list(range(16))  # matches the sweep in the chart above
```

Four illustrative days are picked out of the real data rather than chosen by
hand: the sunniest day, the cloudiest (excluding near-zero days, which are
more likely a sensor outage than genuine weather — even heavy overcast yields
some diffuse light), the most price-volatile, and the one closest to a
typical day by total generation.

```{python}
#| echo: false
sim_with_date = sim.with_columns(pl.col("hour").dt.date().alias("date"))

daily_stats = (
    sim_with_date.group_by("date")
    .agg(
        pl.len().alias("n_hours"),
        pl.col("generation_kwh").sum().alias("daily_generation_kwh"),
        pl.col("price_eur_mwh").std().alias("price_volatility"),
    )
    .filter(pl.col("n_hours") == 24)  # exclude partial days at the data boundary
)

sunny = daily_stats.sort("daily_generation_kwh", descending=True).row(0, named=True)
cloudy = (
    daily_stats.filter(pl.col("daily_generation_kwh") > 1.0)
    .sort("daily_generation_kwh")
    .row(0, named=True)
)
volatile = daily_stats.sort("price_volatility", descending=True).row(0, named=True)
_median_gen = daily_stats["daily_generation_kwh"].median()
typical = (
    daily_stats.with_columns((pl.col("daily_generation_kwh") - _median_gen).abs().alias("d"))
    .sort("d")
    .row(0, named=True)
)

picks = {
    "Sunny day (peak solar)": sunny["date"],
    "Cloudy day (low solar)": cloudy["date"],
    "Volatile price day": volatile["date"],
    "Typical day": typical["date"],
}
label_lookup = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "date": list(picks.values()),
        "day_label": [f"{d} — {desc}" for desc, d in picks.items()],
    }
)
label_lookup
```

The battery's state of charge on any given day depends on its entire history,
so each candidate size is simulated across the **full multi-year series**
(not just the four days below) — the four days are then sliced back out for
charting, keeping the embedded dataset small while keeping the SoC trace
correct.

```{python}
#| echo: false
_gens = sim_with_date["generation_kwh"].to_list()
_loads = sim_with_date["load_kwh"].to_list()
_selected_dates = label_lookup["date"].to_list()

day_frame = pl.concat(
    [
        sim_with_date.with_columns(
            pl.Series("soc_kwh", socs),
            pl.Series("self_consumption_kwh", self_c),
            pl.Series("battery_charge_kwh", charge),
            pl.Series("battery_discharge_kwh", discharge),
            pl.Series("grid_purchase_kwh", grid),
            pl.Series("export_kwh", export),
            pl.lit(b).alias("battery_kwh"),
        ).filter(pl.col("date").is_in(_selected_dates))
        for b in BATTERY_SIZES_KWH
        for socs, self_c, charge, discharge, grid, export in [
            simulate_battery_trace(float(b), _gens, _loads)
        ]
    ]
).join(label_lookup, on="date", how="inner")

usage_long = day_frame.unpivot(
    index=["day_label", "battery_kwh", "hour_of_day"],
    on=["self_consumption_kwh", "battery_discharge_kwh", "grid_purchase_kwh"],
    variable_name="source",
    value_name="kwh",
).with_columns(
    pl.col("source").replace(
        {
            "self_consumption_kwh": "Own use — direct solar",
            "battery_discharge_kwh": "Own use — from battery",
            "grid_purchase_kwh": "Bought from grid",
        }
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
_MAX_BATTERY_KWH = max(BATTERY_SIZES_KWH)
_filter_expr = "datum.day_label == selected_day && datum.battery_kwh == selected_battery_kwh"

day_param = alt.param(
    name="selected_day",
    value=label_lookup.filter(pl.col("date") == sunny["date"])["day_label"][0],
    bind=alt.binding_select(options=label_lookup["day_label"].to_list(), name="Example day: "),
)
battery_param = alt.param(
    name="selected_battery_kwh",
    value=5,
    bind=alt.binding_range(
        min=0, max=_MAX_BATTERY_KWH, step=1, name="Battery size (kWh): "
    ),
)

soc_chart = (
    alt.Chart(day_frame)
    .transform_filter(_filter_expr)
    .mark_area(color="#4C78A8", opacity=0.6, line={"color": "#4C78A8"})
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour of day"),
        y=alt.Y(
            "soc_kwh:Q",
            title="Battery SoC (kWh)",
            scale=alt.Scale(domain=[0, _MAX_BATTERY_KWH]),
        ),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour"),
            alt.Tooltip("soc_kwh:Q", title="SoC (kWh)", format=".2f"),
        ],
    )
    .properties(width="container", height=160)
)

usage_chart = (
    alt.Chart(usage_long)
    .transform_filter(_filter_expr)
    .mark_bar()
    .encode(
        x=alt.X("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour of day"),
        y=alt.Y("kwh:Q", title="Electricity serving load (kWh)"),
        color=alt.Color(
            "source:N",
            title=None,
            scale=alt.Scale(
                domain=["Own use — direct solar", "Own use — from battery", "Bought from grid"],
                range=["#54A24B", "#4C78A8", "#E45756"],
            ),
        ),
        order=alt.Order("source:N"),
        tooltip=[
            alt.Tooltip("hour_of_day:O", title="Hour"),
            alt.Tooltip("source:N", title="Source"),
            alt.Tooltip("kwh:Q", title="kWh", format=".2f"),
        ],
    )
    .properties(width="container", height=220)
)

(soc_chart & usage_chart).add_params(day_param, battery_param)
```

At the default 5 kWh, the battery fills by early afternoon on the sunny day
and then covers most of the evening's demand, leaving only a small grid
purchase overnight. Drag the size to 0 kWh to see the no-battery baseline —
every non-solar hour bought from the grid — or up to 15 kWh to see how much
of the sunny day's export could theoretically be captured with more storage
(with rapidly diminishing returns, matching the savings curve above).

On the cloudy day there's barely enough generation to charge any battery
size, so almost every hour is bought from the grid regardless of the slider.

The volatile-price day turns out to sit inside a week-long *Dunkelflaute*
(dark lull) — generation had already been scarce for days before the price
spiked past €900/MWh, so even a large battery had almost nothing left to give
exactly when it would have been most valuable. A battery that only charges
from solar surplus can't arbitrage a price spike it never got the chance to
prepare for.

## Why timing matters — the midday price dip

Germany-wide PV output depresses the day-ahead price around midday — the
"duck curve" effect. One representative June week:

```{python}
#| echo: false
week = sim.filter(
    (pl.col("hour") >= pl.datetime(2025, 6, 16)) & (pl.col("hour") < pl.datetime(2025, 6, 23))
)

base_week = alt.Chart(week).encode(x=alt.X("hour:T", title="Hour"))

gen_line = base_week.mark_area(opacity=0.4, color="#F2C94C").encode(
    y=alt.Y("generation_kwh:Q", title="PV generation (kWh)"),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("hour:T", title="Hour", format="%a %d %b %H:%M"),
        alt.Tooltip("generation_kwh:Q", title="Generation (kWh)", format=".2f"),
    ],
)
price_line = base_week.mark_line(color="#4C78A8", strokeWidth=2).encode(
    y=alt.Y("price_eur_mwh:Q", title="Day-ahead price (€/MWh)"),
    tooltip=[
        alt.Tooltip("hour:T", title="Hour", format="%a %d %b %H:%M"),
        alt.Tooltip("price_eur_mwh:Q", title="Price (€/MWh)", format=".1f"),
    ],
)

alt.layer(gen_line, price_line).resolve_scale(y="independent").properties(
    width="container", height=280
).configure_view(strokeWidth=0)
```

As printed above, generation and the spot price correlate negatively across
the full window — solar output and price move in opposite directions often
enough that *when* a battery buys and sells matters, not just how much it
can hold.

## Caveats

- **Proxy weather station**: Munich has no DWD radiation station; this uses
  Weihenstephan-Dürnast, ~30 km north.
- **Fixed system size**: 8 kWp / 4,000 kWh load are constants, not sliders —
  the battery simulation is sequential (state-of-charge is path-dependent) and
  can't be recomputed live in the browser, so they're fixed to keep the three
  economic sliders above valid.
- **Synthetic load profile**: a fixed diurnal shape, not a real smart-meter
  reading — no weekday/weekend or seasonal variation.
- **Feed-in tariff applies only to residual export**: the model prices only
  the surplus the battery can't absorb at the statutory FIT, not total
  generation — full-generation spot-market sale isn't representative of real
  German residential PV economics.
- **Solar-only charging**: the battery only ever charges from PV surplus, never
  from cheap grid power — a real dynamic-tariff battery could also arbitrage
  by buying at low overnight prices, which would help precisely during events
  like the Dunkelflaute above.
- **Whole-kWh battery sizes only**: the day-by-day walkthrough precomputes
  0–15 kWh in 1 kWh steps (matching the sweep above) since each size needs its
  own full sequential simulation — intermediate sizes aren't selectable.
